strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear statistical evidence that scientific abstracts have substantially denser nuggets (39.5% vs ~4% in other domains) and more complex event structures than existing datasets
Comprehensive dataset construction: Rigorous multi-stage annotation process with quality control across 2,508 documents and 24,381 events, with detailed schema design grounded in document structure

Strong experimental results: EXCEEDS consistently outperforms baselines on all metrics, with particularly strong hierarchical event extraction (EC F1: 47.60), and thorough analysis of performance across complex nugget types
Principled technical approach: Word-word event grid elegantly unifies encoding of nugget boundaries, event-argument links, and hierarchical relationships in an end-to-end framework

Comprehensive analysis: Detailed statistics on event/argument distributions, complex information forms, and comparison with established benchmarks provides strong motivation for domain-specific methods
weaknesses: Limited dataset scope: Only ACL papers (2019-2022) in NLP domain, not truly 'scientific domain'; only abstracts, not full papers; moderate size (2,508 docs) by modern standards; unclear generalization to other scientific fields (biology, chemistry, physics, medicine)

Missing critical quality metrics: No inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's Kappa) reported; only describes quality inspection procedures without quantitative validation; fundamental requirement for reproducible dataset contributions

Moderate method novelty: Grid-based token-pair relations adapted from prior work [12]; BiAttention and Biaffine are standard techniques; main contribution is combining existing techniques rather than introducing novel concepts

Problematic baseline comparisons: OneIE uses additional entity annotations others lack (unfair); BartGen and PAIE require external ED module; no comparison with recent LLM-based approaches despite claiming they are state-of-the-art; no statistical significance testing despite multiple runs

Inadequate ablation studies: Only ablates Biaffine and BiAttention modules; missing ablations on CLN, BiLSTM, grid design choices, and 3 heuristic inference rules; rules appear ad-hoc without justification (e.g., 'broken HTL chain' undefined)

Unresolved core challenges: Despite design goals, performance on complex nuggets remains poor (inconsecutive F1=25.34, reverse-ordered F1=18.54); these are 4% of nuggets but undermine claims of handling complexity; authors acknowledge difficulty but propose no solutions

Technical presentation issues: Batch size of 1 used without justification; hyperparameter choices (hidden size 1024, learning rates) not explained or ablated; no analysis of computational efficiency; unclear handling of abstracts exceeding BERT token limit

Incomplete reproducibility: Dataset/code promised on GitHub but status unclear; standard deviations/confidence intervals not reported; limited detail on hyperparameter selection; relatively small test set (250 documents)

Missing error analysis: No breakdown of which event types are most problematic; no qualitative case studies of failures; no cross-domain evaluation (news→scientific transfer); no inter-rater reliability on schema validity or environment classification

strengths: Well-motivated dataset contribution: Scientific domain event extraction is understudied; clear characterization of denser nuggets (39.5% vs 3.7-5.7% in other domains) and complex event structures
Rigorous annotation procedure: Three-stage annotation process with expert reviewers, quality control checks, and clear schema design tailored to scientific abstracts
Comprehensive dataset analysis: Good comparative statistics with existing datasets, detailed event type and argument type distributions, documentation of complex phenomena
Novel supplementary metrics: Introduction of event correlation (EC) metric for capturing hierarchical event structures
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Word-word grid approach closely follows prior work (Li et al. 2022 on NER); main modifications are incremental. Stacking existing components (BiLSTM, CLN, BiAttention, Biaffine) lacks clear innovation or justification over alternatives

Concerning performance on core challenges: Complex nuggets show very poor performance (inconsecutive: 17.51 AC F1, reverse-ordered: 10.86 AC F1)—exactly what the method claims to address. This undermines the main contribution

Dataset generalization concerns: Limited to ACL abstracts (2019-2022, single NLP conference). Schema (4-part abstract structure) highly specific to academic papers; no evidence of transferability to other scientific domains, document types, or genres

Evaluation rigor issues: No inter-annotator agreement reported; no statistical significance testing; unfair baseline setup (BartGen/PAIE use external ED module); unusual batch size of 1; missing data quality metrics beyond screening
Incomplete error analysis: No qualitative examples, failure case studies, or per-event-type performance breakdown. Heuristic decoding rules (Section 5.3) vaguely described and appear ad-hoc
Reproducibility gaps: Missing implementation details (random seeds, exact hyperparameter tuning, number of runs), no computational cost analysis, unclear preprocessing steps

Limited baseline comparisons: No sequence labeling baselines, no scientific domain-specific BERT variants (e.g., SciBERT), no document-level EE methods (e.g., DocEE). Weak motivation for EC metric with modest improvements
Scale and scope limitations: 2,508 documents is moderate for a dataset paper (cf. RAMS: 3,993, DocEE: 12,284); schema specificity limits applicability; no cross-domain evaluation

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in event extraction research for scientific domain with rigorous dataset construction (2,508 documents, multi-stage annotation process with quality control)
Comprehensive dataset analysis with meaningful statistics: 40% token density in nuggets vs 4-5% in other domains, 37% non-flat nuggets, 25% sub-events—demonstrating density and complexity claims
State-of-the-art experimental results across all metrics, particularly strong on event correlation (EC F1: 47.60), validating the approach for hierarchical event extraction
Introduces event correlation (EC) metric for evaluating hierarchical/nested events—a useful community contribution
Well-designed word-word grid representation that unifies handling of complex nuggets (overlapped, inconsecutive, reverse-ordered) and hierarchical event structures in a principled framework
Thorough evaluation including complex scenario analysis (Table 4) and ablation studies demonstrating importance of both BiAttention and Biaffine modules
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (CLN, BiAttention, Biaffine) are from prior work [18, 12, 56]; grid representation builds heavily on Li et al. [12]; contribution is primarily in domain application rather than methodological innovation

Critical missing analysis: no inter-annotator agreement (IAA) metrics reported, which is essential for validating dataset quality and schema clarity; this prevents assessment of whether model failures reflect genuine difficulty or ambiguous annotations

Insufficient generalization analysis: dataset limited to ACL papers (2019-2022) from single conference; no cross-domain evaluation on other scientific corpora or subdisciplines (biology, chemistry, etc.); unclear if approach generalizes beyond NLP

Limited error analysis: paper acknowledges inconsecutive and reverse-ordered nuggets are challenging (F1 < 26%) but provides no diagnosis, qualitative examples, or proposed solutions; no systematic breakdown of errors by event/argument type

Unfair baseline comparisons: OneIE uses additional entity annotation during training (footnote 2) while others don't; baselines lack explicit hierarchical event mechanisms, making EXCEEDS' advantage somewhat expected; missing comparisons with recent LLM-based methods (ChatGPT approaches from 2023)

Modest dataset scale (2,508 documents) compared to contemporary large-scale datasets; class imbalance not addressed (1-3% for inconsecutive/reverse-ordered nuggets); no weighted loss or special handling for rare classes

Inference heuristics (three rules in Section 5.3) appear ad-hoc without principled justification; disconnect between end-to-end learning and hard constraints not discussed; no ablation on individual heuristic rules

Computational efficiency not addressed: O(L²) grid complexity with large hidden size (1024) raises scalability concerns for longer documents; no analysis of training time, inference speed, or memory requirements

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of density and complexity challenges specific to scientific event extraction

High-quality dataset contribution (2,508 documents, 24,381 events) with rigorous quality control (73.05% first-pass acceptance), iterative schema refinement with domain experts, and comprehensive annotation protocol documentation

Intuitive and sound technical approach: word-word grid formulation elegantly unifies event detection and argument extraction while naturally handling hierarchical relations, discontinuous arguments, and long-distance dependencies

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 10+ baselines across architectural families, ablation studies, complex scenario analysis, and error analysis revealing that missed predictions dominate over boundary errors
State-of-the-art results with notable improvements on complex structure metrics (AC: +0.51%, EC: +0.53% over second-best baseline)
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: clear writing, extensive appendices with annotation protocol, hyperparameters, full results, and statistical analysis

Comparative analysis demonstrating SciEvents exhibits significantly higher information density (5.54 events, 12.82 arguments per 100 tokens) and more complex structures (33.70% overlapping, 25.63% sub-events) than existing datasets
weaknesses: Severely limited dataset scope: sourced exclusively from ACL conference abstracts (2019-2022) representing only NLP sub-domain; 'scientific domain' claims not validated across chemistry, biology, physics, or other scientific fields; generalizability fundamentally constrained

Core challenge incompletely addressed: despite dense/complex structures being primary motivation, performance on these remains poor (discontinuous: 13.86% F1, overlapping: 22.46% F1, reverse-order: 48.32% F1), suggesting grid formulation has fundamental limitations for stated problems

Critical omission: inter-annotator agreement (IAA) scores not reported; only first-pass inspection rate (73.05%) provided; cannot verify dataset consistency meets standards expected for training/evaluation benchmark

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: O(l²) complexity not contextualized; average document length ~175 tokens means 175×175 grid; behavior for longer documents (l=350+) unclear; training cost (0.0609 GPU hours/epoch) lacks baseline comparison

Methodological design choices lack justification: no explanation for 2D convolutions in grid refinement, no comparison with alternative structured representations (graphs, AMR), heuristic decoding with ontology constraints appears brittle, no sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters (e.g., K=2 refinement layers)

No cross-domain or transfer learning experiments: models trained on SciEvents not evaluated on biomedical/legal/clinical domains despite existing EE datasets; cannot determine if insights specific to ACL abstracts or generalizable to scientific domain; transfers to other domains untested

Limited theoretical justification for grid approach: beyond intuitive appeal, no formal analysis of why grid-based modeling should outperform alternatives; missing ablation comparing simpler pairwise classification; no visualization or interpretation of learned grid patterns

LLM evaluation insufficient: only one LLM baseline (KnowCoder with LLaMA 2-7B); no GPT-3.5/4 prompting experiments; LLMs not given equal tuning effort as EXCEEDS; doesn't reflect practical use cases of commercial LLM APIs

Evaluation metric limitations: exact span matching is strict without partial credit; no macro/micro F1 breakdown by event type; zero-threshold multi-label decision (Eq. 6) simplistic with no threshold sensitivity analysis

Reproducibility gaps: code availability status unclear; annotation tool shown only as Chinese screenshots; data release timeline unspecified; conservative training strategy (skip early validation) could mask convergence issues

Event correlation task feels disconnected: sub-events comprise only 25.63% of dataset; EC improvement smallest among metrics (0.53%); unclear if hierarchical structure is central or peripheral contribution

Limited analysis of why method works: insufficient intuition beyond grid formulation; no explanation for metric-specific improvements; missing qualitative examples showing grid advantages over baselines; no error type comparison with other methods

strengths: Well-constructed dataset with comprehensive annotation quality control (73% first-pass acceptance) and detailed documentation enabling reproducibility
Clear motivation: quantified evidence that scientific texts have higher event density (5.54/100 tokens) and complexity (33.7% overlapping, 25.6% sub-events) than existing EE datasets
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple baseline families, error analysis, complex scenario breakdown, and ablations
Systematic statistical comparison with existing datasets (Tables 1-2) demonstrating distinctive characteristics
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and extensive appendices
weaknesses: Severely limited domain scope undermines claims: only ACL conference abstracts (NLP domain exclusively), not general scientific literature; generalizability to other sciences undemonstrated and likely poor
Abstract-only restriction acknowledged but critical: excludes multi-modal content, figures, tables, cross-references essential to understanding scientific papers

EXCEEDS method lacks technical novelty: word-pair grids extensively explored in recent work (Lou et al. 2023, Liu et al. 2023); standard BiLSTM + 2D convolution + linear classification represents incremental engineering rather than innovation

Method fundamentally fails to address its stated motivation: performance on complex nuggets (discontinuous 13.86%, overlapping 22.46%) represents 50-70% drops from overall 43.2% AC, indicating grid representation does not solve structural complexity as claimed

Marginal and inconsistent empirical results: AC (43.20%) actually worse than PAIE baseline (43.92%); only EC shows modest +0.53% improvement; no statistical significance testing despite overlapping standard deviations

Critical missing annotation metrics: no inter-annotator agreement (IAA/Cohen's Kappa) reported; only 73% first-pass acceptance given without analysis of systematic disagreement patterns; fine-grained schema (10 event types, 20 argument types) correlates with high type confusion errors (Figure 5)

Unfair experimental setup: discriminative models evaluated only on contiguous nuggets despite 33.7% overlapping nuggets in test set; generative models required interface modifications; global models leveraged entity information—creates incomparable baselines

Incomplete ablation studies: only tests contextual encoding and grid refiner; does not ablate HTL/THL/EAL designs, convolution kernels, refinement layer count, or provide per-event-type performance analysis

Diagnosis absent for core failures: no explanation why grid method underperforms on overlapping nuggets or how to address documented challenges; error analysis (Figure 4) categorizes but doesn't diagnose root causes

Dataset scalability concerns: 2,508 documents is modest compared to recent datasets (RAMS 9,124, PHEE 4,827); O(l²) grid complexity limits application to long documents; no evidence of transfer to other scientific domains or corpus expansion potential

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of scientific text characteristics (density and complexity) empirically validated through systematic dataset comparison
High-quality dataset construction with rigorous quality control (73.05% first-pass acceptance rate), careful schema design through expert iteration, and exceptional reproducibility documentation
Elegant grid-based technical formulation (HTL/THL/EAL) that provides unified representation for complex nuggets, hierarchical events, and document-level multi-event modeling
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 10 baselines across three architecture families, extended metrics (event correlation), detailed error analysis, and ablation studies

Substantial dataset scale (24,381 events, 56,411 arguments) reflecting information-intensive nature rather than schema expansion, with rich complexity annotations (overlapping 33.70%, sub-events 25.63%)
Exceptional attention to reproducibility with detailed implementation information, computational complexity analysis, and promise of public release
weaknesses: Limited dataset scope: abstract-only collection from single subdomain (ACL/NLP), restricting to concise summaries and excluding full papers, figures, tables, and other scientific disciplines—undermines claims about general scientific EE

Core challenges remain substantially unresolved: performance on complex structures significantly lower (discontinuous 13.86%, overlapping 22.46% AC vs. 43.20% overall), indicating grid formulation doesn't adequately address identified density+complexity problems

Moderate technical novelty: grid-based formulation is clean but incremental application of known techniques; 2D convolutions for refinement are standard; decoding relies on ad-hoc heuristics suggesting potential brittleness

Modest absolute performance (43.20% AC, 48.25% EC F1-scores) with no human performance baselines or inter-annotator agreement for context; unclear if scores reflect task difficulty or method limitations

Limited generalization evidence: evaluated only on SciEvents with no cross-dataset evaluation, out-of-domain testing, or performance analysis on existing EE benchmarks; cannot assess whether grid approach generalizes

Conservative training strategy (skipping early validation due to exponential chain explosion in decoding) suggests optimization challenges; pruning-based decoding heuristics (HTL/THL chain validation) lack theoretical justification
Insufficient analysis of why complex structures remain challenging despite specialized design; error analysis limited to distributions without qualitative investigation of failure modes
